title: The LORD Who Avenges and Shelters
sum: The book opens with its title (an oracle about Nineveh, a vision of Nahum) and a hymn. The LORD is a jealous God who takes vengeance, slow to anger but never leaving guilt unpunished. He comes in gale and storm, dries the sea and rivers, shakes the mountains and burns like fire. At the center is a single line of comfort: the LORD is good, a stronghold in a day of trouble, and he knows those who shelter in him.

Then the speech turns to a plotter against the LORD who comes out of a city, and to a "you" whose yoke the LORD will snap. It ends with a runner on the mountains (1:15), the herald of Isaiah 52:7, telling Judah to keep its festivals and pay its vows because the worthless one will never pass through again. The chapter is the book's argument in miniature: the God who protects is the God who ends an empire.
readings: Read as a hymn to the divine warrior

1:2-8 is the kind of poem that Israel sang to the LORD as king of nature and of history (compare Psalms 18, 29, 97 and Habakkuk 3). It stands apart from the oracle that follows and may once have been a separate song, perhaps with a partial alphabetic frame. Read this way the opening sets the terms: whoever stands against the LORD cannot stand, and whoever shelters in him is known.
Read as a word for Judah under Assyria

Judah had paid tribute to Assyria for about a century. Verses 12-15 speak to a small kingdom that has been brought low and is told the yoke will break. Seen so, the whole chapter is comfort for the afflicted and a warning to the oppressor, and the "vengeance" of 1:2 is the justice for which the oppressed prayed.

Nahum 1:3 quotes the creed of Exodus 34:6-7 as Jonah 4:2 and Joel 2:13 do, but keeps only "slow to anger" and "will not leave guilt unpunished." The same creed in Jonah explains why Nineveh was spared, and in Nahum why it is not spared now.

views.H: The setting is Judah between the sack of Thebes (about 663 BC) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC), with the yoke of Assyria still on Judah's neck (1:13). Whether this is Manasseh's long reign or the weakening of Assyria in Josiah's early years is debated. Josephus (Antiquities 9.11.3) puts Nahum in Jotham's time, about 115 years before the fall; that does not fit Thebes, which Nahum 3:8 treats as already fallen.
views.C: The chapter raises the book's critical questions. Is 1:2-8 a separate, partial acrostic hymn joined to the oracle (Gunkel 1893; Christensen 1975) or part of one composition? Who is addressed in 1:9-14, and is 1:12-13 about Judah or Nineveh? Is 1:15 an addition (it matches Isaiah 52:7) or the original beginning of a victory song? Alfred Haldar (1947) read the book as a liturgy by a cult prophet. The text is hard at 1:9-10, 12 and 14.
views.J: The Hebrew Bible counts Nahum among the Twelve, one scroll (Bava Batra 13b-15a), with Nahum next after Micah. The notes of this edition quote no passage of the Targum, Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Radak on Nahum 1, which were not checked; the Jewish lens here is limited to the order and unity of the Twelve and to the link between 1:15 and Isaiah 52:7 that the Hebrew words themselves show.
views.X: Paul's use of Isaiah 52:7 in Romans 10:15 gave the herald's feet a place in the church's talk of preaching. Calvin's lectures on Nahum read the opening verses as set before the afflicted Israelites so that they know God cares about their suffering (on 1:2), read 1:7 as showing that God's goodness is not cancelled by his severity, and read the herald of 1:15 as heralds of peace who can now speak freely on the mountains because Assyria's rule is ending. Which church fathers read Nahum 1:15 as the preaching of the gospel was not checked here. The puzzle for many readers is a book of vengeance after Jonah's mercy.

deep.h: Dating Nahum: between Thebes and Nineveh
deep.b: Nahum 3:8-10 speaks of the fall of Thebes as past, so the book is later than about 663 BC, when Ashurbanipal sacked it. The fall of Nineveh in 612 BC is the other limit, though the book describes it as coming and not as done. Between the two, the commonest estimates fall in two groups. 650s to 630s: Assyria is still at its height, Judah is a vassal (1:13), and the oracle foretells a fall few could believe. 630s to 612: Assyria is weaker (Ashurbanipal died about 631) and Babylon and the Medes are rising; the book's graphic account of the siege fits the last years. A few read the vivid detail of chapter 2 as written after the event. The Plain English Translation takes the date as unknown within this range.

The Hebrew speaks to "you" in the plural (1:9) and the singular (1:11-15), and about "he" and "they." The singular "you" changes gender: feminine in 1:11-13 and 1:15, masculine in 1:14. The feminine fits either Nineveh (as in 2:1 and 3:5) or Judah (1:15), and the book does not say which. The masculine of 1:14 ("your name," "your gods," "your grave") is addressed to a man, most naturally the Assyrian king or the worthless adviser of 1:11 and 1:15. One path: 1:9-11 to Nineveh (what are you plotting? a plotter has come out of you), 1:12-13 to Judah (I brought you low; I will break his yoke off you), 1:14 to the king, and 1:15 to Judah. Another keeps all of it on Judah's side. The Plain English Translation follows the shifts as the Hebrew has them and does not name the person addressed.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a book built on the words of its opening hymn
deep.b: The words that carry the hymn come back at the end, turned. Ma'oz ("stronghold") is the LORD for those who shelter in him (1:7) and the thing Nineveh will look for in vain (3:11). The verb 'avar ("pass over") is the flood (1:8) and the plotter (1:12, 15) and finally Nineveh's own wickedness (3:19). Nacham ("comfort") gives the prophet his name and leaves Nineveh with no comforters (3:7). "Look, I am against you" frames the second half (2:13; 3:5). If this is deliberate, the book's end is the hymn's argument carried out. I offer it as my own observation; it overlaps with literary readings of Nahum (Sweeney; O'Brien) but is not taken from them.

echoes: Exodus 34:6-7; Exodus 14:21; Joshua 3:16; Deuteronomy 32:35, 41; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 94:1; Isaiah 10:5; Isaiah 14:25; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 40:9; Romans 10:15; Romans 12:19; Malachi 3:2; Revelation 6:17

settings.what: The opening hymn: the LORD as warrior and refuge
settings.by: Nahum of Elkosh, as the heading presents him
settings.to: Judah is the likeliest first audience (the commonest view), though the heading addresses the oracle "about Nineveh"
settings.when: after the fall of Thebes (about 663 BC) and before the fall of Nineveh (612 BC); the exact time is debated
settings.why: To tell Judah, who had paid tribute to Assyria for a century, that the God who made the sea and the mountains is a jealous, avenging judge, and a refuge for those who trust him. It sets the rule for the rest of the book: no power stands before him, and no one who shelters in him is overlooked.
views: Judah in the shadow of Assyria
Comfort for a vassal kingdom and warning to its oppressor.
Alfred Haldar thought the book was a cult prophet's liturgy; the hymn would then be sung in worship.
Gunkel and many since treat 1:2-8 as an older song, partly in alphabetical order, that the oracle uses.

settings.what: The plotters and the broken yoke
settings.by: The LORD, as the prophet reports him
settings.to: Nineveh and Judah in turn, and in 1:14 a male figure (the king or the plotter); the Hebrew shifts addressees without a label
settings.when: the same time as the hymn
settings.why: To say to Assyria that its plots against the LORD will end, and to say to Judah that its affliction is over. Knowing the shifts changes the reading: 1:12-13 is the nearest the book comes to speaking directly to Judah's pain.
views: Nineveh in 1:9-11, Judah in 1:12-13, a king in 1:14
The commonest solution, with the masculine "you" of 1:14 taken as the Assyrian king or the plotter.
A few read the "you" of 1:9-11 as Judeans who doubt the LORD.

settings.when: in the vision, after the plotter is "cut off"
settings.why: To tell Judah the news has come and to call it to its festivals and vows. In Judah's reading, the end of Assyria's rule restores the right of pilgrimage and worship. Its words match Isaiah 52:7.

traditions.q: How do the churches read the language of God's vengeance? (1:2-8)
views: Aquinas teaches that God's justice and mercy do not oppose each other: mercy does not destroy justice but is a kind of fullness of it (Summa Theologiae I, q. 21, a. 3, ad 2).

Isaac the Syrian, a seventh-century bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East whom the Orthodox also honor as a saint, taught that God's love is not turned into hatred by punishment: those who resist it feel it as torment (Mystic Treatises; the treatise is not identified here). Other Orthodox writers and the liturgy keep the language of God's wrath.
Luther's Large Catechism reads God's jealousy and punishment in Exodus 20:5 as threat and promise together: he is angry at those who despise him and gracious to those who keep his commandments.

The Westminster Confession (2.1) calls God "most just, and terrible in his judgments, hating all sin, and who will by no means clear the guilty," in the words of Exodus 34:7 and Nahum 1:3. Calvin, on Nahum 1:2, says the prophet opens with God's nature so that the doom of Nineveh will carry weight, and that the vengeance is declared because Nineveh wronged God's people; he also warns that human feelings must not be imagined in God.

title: The Destroyer Comes
sum: The attacker is at the gates. The prophet speaks to Nineveh with a defender's orders (guard the fort, watch the road, brace yourselves), then paints the assault: red shields, scarlet clothes, chariots like torches in the squares. The river gates open, the palace caves in, the city is uncovered and carried off, and the slave girls mourn like doves. The city that was like a pool of water is emptied. Its silver and gold are looted, and the people lose heart.

Then a funeral song asks where the lions' lair has gone, the lair where the lion brought prey for his cubs and no one scared them. The chapter closes with the LORD's own challenge: "Look, I am against you." Chariots go up in smoke, the sword eats the young lions, and the voice of the city's messengers will never be heard again.
readings: Told from outside, with taunts, sound and color, as a song of those freed from Assyria. The speaker delights in the picture of the proud brought down.

The questions ("Where is the lions' lair now?") and the details of grief (the mourning slave girls) are the language of lament. The same poet mourns the city he is condemning, or at least speaks in the form of mourning.

The picture fits what is known of 612 BC: a siege, a water attack, fire and plunder (Babylonian Chronicle). The poem is not a report and the Plain English Translation does not use the Chronicle to fill it in.

views.H: The attackers are most likely the Babylonians and the Medes (612 BC). The Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 3) gives the siege (about three months), the fall in the month of Ab, and the carrying off of the city's spoil. Excavations at Nineveh's gates show burning and fighting. Diodorus' flood story (from Ctesias) is late and not a source of the Plain English Translation.
views.C: Nahum 2 is the poem most often cited for the book's art: sound, color and speed. Critical questions: how much is vision of the future and how much description of the event; the hard words of 2:3, 2:5-8 (peladot, the covering, Huzzab); whether 2:13 closes the chapter or begins the next section. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew at each and says where the Greek differs.
views.J: The Hebrew chapter begins at English 1:15: "Look, on the mountains," and so opens on peace for Judah. The Nahum Pesher from Qumran takes the lion passage of 2:11-13 to refer to a later king, the "Lion of Wrath," most often identified with Alexander Jannaeus. Medieval Jewish commentators on this chapter were not checked for this edition.
views.X: Calvin's lecture on 2:1 sets out two readings of the "destroyer": one refers it to Sennacherib, whom God scattered "like smoke," and one makes the destroyer Nebuchadnezzar coming against the Assyrians. The church fathers on this chapter were not checked for this edition. The graphic violence is the part many readers today find hardest.

deep.b: Assyrian kings called themselves lions, and Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh has carved reliefs of him hunting lions on foot and from a chariot, the king's killing of the animal shown as the proof of his rule. Nahum turns the picture around: the lions' den is now empty and the lion has no one to scare. Jeremiah 50:17 uses the same figure for Assyria's devouring of Israel. The Qumran commentary on Nahum (4Q169) applies the lion to a Jewish king of the first century BC. The Plain English Translation keeps four different Hebrew lion words apart in 2:11-13 and the notes say which.

Sennacherib (705-681 BC) rebuilt Nineveh and enclosed it with a wall about eight miles around, pierced by many gates, and brought water to it by canals and a stone aqueduct. These works make Nahum's water images (the river gates, the pool) fit a real city, and they make the defender's orders at 2:1 grimly sensible. The Hebrew describes sound and speed more than layout, so the Plain English Translation does not try to draw a map.

echoes: Jeremiah 50:17; Jeremiah 51:30; Isaiah 24:1; Isaiah 33:1; Joel 2:6; Zephaniah 2:13-15; Habakkuk 2:8; Daniel 7:4

settings.to: Nineveh is addressed ("Guard the fort"); Judah overhears
settings.when: in vision, shortly before the fall in 612 BC, or with the fall in view
settings.why: To show Judah the fall of the empire as already happening, and to Nineveh that its defenses are useless. For the first hearers this is a victory song: the one who has scattered others is scattered. Knowing the hearers changes the reading: the violence is described by people who suffered it.
views: The oracle was given before the fall.
The poem was written after, in the form of a prediction.
The poem was spoken in worship, as a ritual of victory (Haldar).

settings.what: The lions' den and the LORD's challenge
settings.to: Nineveh, in the style of a funeral song; the last verse is the LORD speaking to the city
settings.why: To say that the empire fed on others and to announce that the LORD himself now stands against it. The "Look, I am against you" is the formula of challenge and is repeated at 3:5.

title: Woe to the City of Bloodshed
sum: Chapter 3 is the funeral song. "Woe to the city of bloodshed," full of lies and loot, with the whip, the wheels and the heaps of dead. The city is a charming prostitute and a mistress of sorceries who sells nations. The LORD is against her and will lift her skirts over her face and show the nations her shame; everyone will say, "Nineveh is ruined," and no one will comfort her.

Then Thebes, strong behind the Nile and backed by Cush, Egypt, Put and Libya, still went into exile and her babies were smashed. Nineveh will do the same. Her fortresses are early figs, her people women, her gates open. She may bring water and mud for a siege, and multiply like locusts, but the fire and sword will find her. The shepherds sleep, the people are scattered, the wound has no cure, and all who hear clap their hands. The last words are a question: has anyone escaped her wickedness?
readings: The charge is bloodshed, lies, looting and the sale of nations. Seen so, the destruction is the answer the oppressed had asked for, and the book ends with the last word to the victims. Critics answer that the text still has God, speaking in the first person, do the stripping and shaming (3:5-7), which gives the violence a divine author.

The picture of a woman stripped and shamed, the smashing of children, and the taunt that the people of the city are women are among the hardest passages in the Twelve. They are part of the book's world and the Plain English Translation does not hide them. Readers and critics (Weems, O'Brien, Yee) ask what it means for God to be pictured doing what the text condemns when others do it.

Jonah ends with a question to the prophet about whether God should not pity Nineveh. Nahum ends with a question to Nineveh about whether anyone escaped its wickedness. The two books together ask what mercy is for, and what happens when it is spent.

views.H: Thebes fell about 663 BC, which gives the book's earliest date. The Assyrian army had taken it and its temples; Nineveh would be taken in 612. The locust figures fit a world where locusts could eat a whole harvest. The "women" taunt (3:13) has parallels in the treaty curses studied by Hillers; the early figs of 3:12 are a picture of easy capture, not a treaty curse. Excavations at Nineveh show burning at the gates.
views.C: Critical questions: the relation of 3:8-10 to the fall of Thebes (the earliest date), the "you" of 3:9, the hard Hebrew in 3:17, the violence of 3:5-7, and whether the book was shaped by later editors into a unit with Jonah and with the Twelve. O'Brien and Weems press the question of the gender of the imagery. Sweeney and Nogalski treat Nahum as a stage in a longer story of Assyria in the Twelve.
views.J: In the Hebrew order Nahum follows Micah, with Jonah earlier; in the Greek order Jonah comes immediately before Nahum. The question at the end of Nahum (3:19) and the question at the end of Jonah (4:11) are often read together in studies of the Twelve (Sweeney; Nogalski). Medieval Jewish commentators on this chapter were not checked for this edition.
views.X: Revelation 17-18 shares the image of a city as a prostitute and sorceress (Revelation 18:23 echoes Nahum 3:4); whether the church fathers read Nahum's city that way was not checked here. A common Christian explanation of why Nahum follows Jonah is that Nineveh repented and later fell back into its evil; which fathers say so was not checked. On the use of force, the confessional answers are set side by side in the card below.

deep.b: Nahum asks Nineveh, "Are you any better than Thebes?" Thebes (No' 'Amon, "city of Amun") was Egypt's old southern capital. Ashurbanipal's army sacked it about 663 BC, and his annals list the loot, among it two great obelisks. For Nahum it was the example of a great, well-defended city that fell. This is why the book cannot be earlier than 663 BC. It also tells us how the prophet saw the matter: he does not need to be told of Assyria's cruelty to Thebes; he uses it against Assyria.

deep.h: A woman, a prostitute, and what the text does
deep.b: Chapter 3 pictures Nineveh as a woman: a charming prostitute, a mistress of sorceries who sells nations, stripped and shown, with the people in her midst called "women." The picture is a standard prophetic one (Hosea 2; Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 13; Ezekiel 16, 23; Lamentations), used of Israel, Judah, Tyre, Babylon and others. Critics (Weems, Yee, O'Brien) say it makes the stripping and shaming of women into a picture of God's justice and so can legitimate the abuse of real women; they point out that the speaker is God, in the first person ("I will uncover your skirts"), which gives the violence a divine author. Others reply that it is a stock figure from ancient warfare, where the humiliation of a captured city's women was real and was done by conquerors, and that the text uses it to describe the aggressor's fall. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The notes give the views, and name a writer only for what that writer's book argues.
deep.refs: Nahum 3:4-7; Hosea 2:10; Isaiah 47:3; Jeremiah 13:26; Ezekiel 16:37; Lamentations 1:8

deep.h: Locusts and the end of the empire
deep.b: The locust figure comes three ways in 3:15-17. The fire and sword eat the city as locusts eat a field. The city is told to multiply like locusts, which is mockery: the more they multiply, the more food for the fire. And her officials are like locusts on a cold wall, gone with the sun. The words are yeleq and 'arbeh and a swarm; the Plain English Translation's Joel term for yeleq, "the hopping locust," is kept (see Joel 1:4).

echoes: Jonah 1:2; Jonah 4:11; Isaiah 23:15-17; Isaiah 47:3; Jeremiah 13:26; Jeremiah 30:12; Jeremiah 46:25; Ezekiel 16:37; Ezekiel 22:2; Ezekiel 24:6; Hosea 2:10; Revelation 17:1-6; Revelation 18:23

settings.what: Woe to the city of bloodshed
settings.when: in the same vision, as the attack closes
settings.why: To name the city's guilt (blood, lies, plunder, sale of nations) and to announce the shame the LORD will bring on it. For the first hearers this answers the question every vassal asked, whether the empire's cruelty would be answered; the hard images are those of the ancient world's treatment of captured cities. The speaker of 3:5-7 is the LORD himself, who is made the agent of the shaming, and critics (Weems, Yee, O'Brien) press that point.
views: The speaker mocks and rejoices (a victory taunt).
The woe-cry (hoy) is the mourner's cry; the speaker mourns what is lost, even as he condemns.

settings.why: To drive the point home with a case everyone knew: a city behind water, with Cush and Egypt as allies, fell to Assyria, and Nineveh will fall the same way. The case of Thebes tells Nineveh that no wall, river or alliance helps.

settings.what: Siege commands, locusts, shepherds and a wound
settings.when: at the end of the vision
settings.why: To mock every defense (water, bricks, numbers) and to end by saying that the empire's leaders sleep, its people are scattered, its wound has no cure, and all who hear of its fall applaud. The last question puts Nineveh's wickedness against the mercy of Jonah.

traditions.q: Does the judgment pictured on Nineveh say anything about Christians using force? (3:1-7)
views: The Catechism does not mention Nahum. It teaches that governments have the right of lawful defense and the duty to work to avoid war, and it sets strict conditions for using military force: lasting, grave and certain damage; every other means shown to be impractical; serious prospects of success; no graver evils than the harm to be removed (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2308-2309).

Basil the Great's Letter 188, canon 13, which the Orthodox Church keeps among its canons, says the fathers did not count killing in war as murder, yet advises those who have killed to keep from communion for three years.

Luther distinguishes God's own judgment from the sword the civil government bears; the soldier may serve his lord, and the church leaves vengeance to God and to rulers in their office (Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved).
The Westminster Confession (23.2) teaches that a Christian may hold the office of magistrate and that, under the New Testament, the magistrate may lawfully wage war on just and necessary occasion.

The Second London Confession (1689, chapter 24) gives the magistrate's sword the same place as the Westminster Confession. Baptists are not of one mind on war today; the one text cited here is the 1689 confession.

The Schleitheim Confession (1527, article 6) holds that the sword is an ordinance of God outside the perfection of Christ, and the Dordrecht Confession (1632, article XIV, on revenge) forbids Christians all revenge and the repaying of evil for evil.
